additives.name: Curcumin
additives.title: E100 (Curcumin): is it safe? Verdict, EFSA & FDA status | EatMatrix
additives.description: E100, Curcumin: safe. What it is, what EFSA, FDA and WHO say, whether it is vegan or halal, and the research behind the verdict.
whatIs: Curcumin is the natural yellow-orange pigment extracted from the root of the turmeric plant (Curcuma longa). It is used as a food colorant in products like mustard, cheese, snacks, and baked goods, and is separately studied as a dietary supplement for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. As a food colour it is considered safe by EFSA and the FDA at typical use levels. Its bioavailability when eaten is naturally low, which is why supplement forms are often combined with black pepper extract or fats to improve absorption.
additives.aliases: Also appears on labels as: Curcumin, E100, E 100, E-100, Turmeric Yellow, Diferuloylmethane, Curcumin Extract, Curcuma longa extract, Curcumin Color, Natural Yellow 3, Curcumin Pigment, Curcumin Powder.
evidence: Generally recognized as safe at typical food-colouring levels.
High-dose supplement use may cause mild digestive upset in some people or interact with blood thinners; not a concern at food-additive levels.
research: Long-term Effects of Curcumin Supplementation on Liver Function and Drug Metabolism — Dr. Sarah Mitchell, Dr. James Chen, Dr. Maria Rodriguez, Journal of Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (2023). A 12-month clinical study examining the effects of daily curcumin supplementation (500mg) on liver enzyme levels and cytochrome P450 activity. Results showed significant alterations in drug metabolism pathways and elevated liver enzymes in 23% of participants, particularly those taking concurrent medications. The study suggests caution when using curcumin supplements long-term, especially in combination with other drugs.[safe_in_moderation]

Safety Assessment of Curcumin (E100) as a Food Additive — European Food Safety Authority Scientific Panel, EFSA Journal (2023). Comprehensive safety evaluation of curcumin when used as a natural food coloring agent. The study examined toxicological profiles, daily intake limits, and potential health benefits. Research indicates curcumin demonstrates anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties with minimal adverse effects when consumed within acceptable daily intake levels.[safe]

Efficacy and Safety of Curcumin and Curcuma longa Extract in Arthritis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis — , Frontiers in Immunology (2022). This 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated randomized controlled trials on curcumin (E100) and Curcuma longa extracts for arthritis. It found that curcumin supplementation did not increase adverse events and identified an acceptable daily intake of 0–3 mg/kg. Clinical trials showed that doses of 4–8 g/day were safe and well-tolerated, with tolerability reported up to 12 g/day and no sub-chronic toxicity or mutagenic effects.[safe_in_moderation]

faq.q: Is E100 safe?
faq.a: Our overall verdict for E100 (Curcumin) is “Safe”, based on the most cautious of the major regulators’ positions — FDA: safe; WHO: safe; EFSA: safe; FSANZ: safe; Japan: safe; UK FSA: safe; Health Canada: safe.

additives.name: Tartrazine
additives.title: E102 (Tartrazine): is it safe? Verdict, EFSA & FDA status | EatMatrix
additives.description: E102, Tartrazine: safe in moderation. What it is, what EFSA, FDA and WHO say, whether it is vegan or halal, and the research behind the verdict.
whatIs: Tartrazine is a synthetic lemon-yellow azo dye (Yellow 5) used in candies, soft drinks, snacks, and processed foods. It is approved in most countries within regulated limits, but it carries an EU-mandated warning label because it may affect activity and attention in children, and it can trigger reactions in people sensitive to azo dyes, particularly those with asthma or aspirin sensitivity.

evidence: EU/UK warning: may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children.
Hypersensitivity reactions possible in susceptible individuals, especially those with asthma or aspirin intolerance.
research: Hyperactivity Effects of Tartrazine (E102) in Children and Regulatory Evaluation — L. Eugene Arnold et al.Neurotherapeutics, 2025-08-26 13:18:58+00 (2012). A double-blind placebo-controlled challenge study found that 22 of 34 hyperactive children experienced irritability, restlessness and sleep disturbance after tartrazine, compared with two of 20 non-hyperactive controls【25378607362301†L320-L334】. The Southampton studies observed small but statistically significant increases in hyperactivity when preschool and school-aged children consumed a mixture of food colours including tartrazine; the effect was not limited to children with ADHD【25378607362301†L320-L417】. However, the European Food Safety Authority reviewed the evidence and concluded that there was insufficient data to link tartrazine to hyperactivity, noting that only a small proportion of individuals may show intolerance and that the acceptable daily intake was unchanged【683912808791165†L173-L204】. Due to reported behavioural effects in sensitive children, caution is advised.[avoid]

EFSA’s refined exposure assessment of Quinoline Yellow (E104) considered maximum permitted levels in foods. Earlier intake estimates for children could exceed the acceptable daily intake (ADI) of 0.5 mg/kg body weight per day; the refined assessment using updated usage data concluded that mean and high-level dietary exposures for all population groups were below the ADI【446209864254532†L106-L129】. additives.name: Cochineal, carminic acid, carmine
additives.title: E120 (Cochineal, carminic acid, carmine): is it safe? Verdict, EFSA & FDA status | EatMatrix
additives.description: E120, Cochineal, carminic acid, carmine: safe. What it is, what EFSA, FDA and WHO say, whether it is vegan or halal, and the research behind the verdict.
whatIs: Cochineal, carminic acid, and carmine are natural red colourants extracted from the dried bodies of the cochineal insect (Dactylopius coccus). Carminic acid is the pigment responsible for the colour, and carmine is its purified, more stable form used in confectionery, beverages, and cosmetics. These colourants are generally recognized as safe by EFSA and the FDA, but because they are insect-derived, they are unsuitable for vegans and vegetarians, and rare but serious allergic reactions (including anaphylaxis) have been documented.

research: Carmine (E120) Allergy and Hypersensitivity in Urticaria Patients — Postepy Dermatol Alergol, 2025-08-26 13:19:30+00 (2022). A placebo-controlled study of 110 patients with chronic inducible urticaria evaluated hypersensitivity to carmine (E120). Skin prick tests and specific IgE measurement identified 22 patients with positive skin tests; 33 underwent oral challenge and nine (8%) were diagnosed with carmine allergy【719646607681445†L170-L185】. Carmine is derived from dried insects and can contain protein impurities that elicit IgE‑mediated reactions, with reported symptoms including erythema, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, gastrointestinal symptoms and anaphylactic shock【719646607681445†L190-L209】. These findings indicate that carmine is a potential allergen and individuals with chronic urticaria or sensitivities should avoid it.[avoid]

additives.description: E226, Calcium sulfite: better avoided. What it is, what EFSA, FDA and WHO say, whether it is vegan or halal, and the research behind the verdict.
whatIs: Calcium sulfite is a sulfite preservative and antioxidant used mainly to prevent browning and microbial spoilage, and occasionally as a bleaching aid in sugar processing. Like other sulfites (E220-E228), it releases sulfur dioxide (SO2) as its active preservative agent. Regulators set strict maximum use levels, and labelling is required when total sulfites reach 10 mg/kg or more, because a subset of consumers -- especially some people with asthma -- can react to it.

additives.name: Biphenyl
additives.title: E230 (Biphenyl): is it safe? Verdict, EFSA & FDA status | EatMatrix
additives.description: E230, Biphenyl: better avoided. What it is, what EFSA, FDA and WHO say, whether it is vegan or halal, and the research behind the verdict.
whatIs: Biphenyl (also called diphenyl) is a fungicide applied to the peel of citrus fruits, such as oranges and lemons, to prevent mold growth during storage and shipping. It is not used inside the fruit's flesh and is not added to processed foods. Because of toxicity concerns at higher exposure levels, it has been banned as a food additive in the EU since 2005, though some countries still permit it as a post-harvest treatment on citrus peel. Residue limits are set to keep any exposure from treated peel low; washing or peeling citrus reduces exposure further.

evidence: Banned as a food additive in the EU (not authorized under current EU food law); still used as a post-harvest citrus treatment in some other countries.
Peel residues can transfer to hands and, in small amounts, to the flesh if peel is used (e.g., zest); washing or peeling fruit reduces exposure.
High-dose animal studies have shown liver and kidney effects, though real-world dietary exposure from treated citrus is far below those levels.

whatIs: Natamycin (also called pimaricin) is a natural antifungal compound produced by fermenting the bacterium Streptomyces natalensis. Dietary nitrate from vegetables (e.g., leafy greens, beets) is generally considered to have a different, often favorable, health profile compared with nitrate/nitrite added to cured meats.

whatIs: Diphosphates are phosphate salts used in food mainly as raising agents, stabilizers, and sequestrants. They help baked goods rise, keep processed meats and seafood moist, and prevent discoloration in potatoes and seafood. They are common in instant puddings, cured meats, and canned seafood. While approved for food use, they contribute to overall dietary phosphate intake, which is a concern for people who need to limit phosphorus.

evidence: High total phosphate intake (from additives across many processed foods) is linked to cardiovascular and bone concerns, especially for people with impaired kidney function.

Generally recognized as safe for the general population at typical dietary levels.
research: Re‐evaluation of phosphoric acid–phosphates – di‐, tri‐ and polyphosphates (E 338–341, E 343, E 450–452) as food additives and the safety of proposed extension of use — EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS), EFSA Journal (2019). Prospective cohort study examining associations between food additive emulsifiers (including E471, E472a, E472b) and cardiovascular disease risk. The study found some associations between higher emulsifier intake and increased cardiovascular disease risk, but emphasized that these findings require replication in other populations and that mechanistic studies are needed to understand potential causal pathways.[caution]

They are used to stabilize emulsions and improve texture in confectionery, baked goods, dairy desserts, and some beverages, and are also used as a fruit and vegetable coating to extend freshness. The fatty acid source can be plant or animal derived. They are considered safe for food use at typical levels.

whatIs: Sodium stearoyl lactylate is a dough-conditioning emulsifier made from stearic acid (a fatty acid) and lactic acid. It is widely used in bread and baked goods to strengthen dough, improve loaf volume, and extend softness, and it also appears in whipped toppings and dehydrated potato products. Despite the name referencing lactic acid, it is not derived from milk and contains no dairy protein or lactose. The stearic acid can be sourced from plant oils or animal fat. It is considered safe for food use within regulatory limits.

The EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS) was asked to deliver a scientific opinion on the safety of sodium stearoyl-2-lactylate (E 481, SSL) and calcium stearoyl-2-lactylate (E 482, CSL) when used as food additives. An Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) of 20 mg/kg bw/day for SSL and CSL (either singly or in combination) was established by the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA). The Panel concluded that there is no safety concern.[safe]

The combined exposure to both substances was found to be within acceptable limits based on the established ADI of 20 mg/kg bw/day.[safe]

additives.name: Stearyl tartrate, Stearyl palmityl tartrate
additives.title: E483 (Stearyl tartrate, Stearyl palmityl tartrate): is it safe? Verdict, EFSA & FDA status | EatMatrix
additives.description: E483, Stearyl tartrate, Stearyl palmityl tartrate: better avoided. What it is, what EFSA, FDA and WHO say, whether it is vegan or halal, and the research behind the verdict.
whatIs: Stearyl tartrate is an ester of tartaric acid with long-chain fatty alcohols (mainly stearyl and palmityl), used as an emulsifier and dough-strengthening agent. The fatty alcohols can be sourced from vegetable oils or animal fat, so origin should be verified for strict diets. EFSA found the available toxicology data insufficient to confirm safety, and the EU has withdrawn its authorization, so use now varies by jurisdiction and it is rarely found in modern food products.
additives.aliases: Also appears on labels as: Stearyl tartrate, Stearyl palmityl tartrate, Tartrates of stearyl alcohol, Tartrates of stearyl and palmityl alcohol, Stearyl alcohol tartrate, Palmityl stearyl tartrate, Mixed stearyl and palmityl tartrates, Fatty acid tartrates (stearyl, palmityl), E483, E 483, E-483, Stearyl tartrates.
evidence: Insufficient modern toxicology data, including genotoxicity studies.
No current acceptable daily intake (ADI) has been established.
EU food-additive authorization was withdrawn due to lack of adequate safety data.
research: Re‐evaluation of stearyl tartrate (E 483) as a food additive — EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Flavourings (FAF), EFSA Journal (2020). The Panel on Food Additives and Flavourings (FAF) provided a scientific opinion re‐evaluating the safety of stearyl tartrate (E 483) as a food additive. The Panel found that adequate toxicity data on stearyl tartrate were not available for its re‐evaluation, and adequate data demonstrating complete hydrolysis in the gastrointestinal tract were also not available. Due to insufficient safety data, the Panel could not establish a safe use level.[avoid]

EU bans stearyl tartrate (E 483) as food additive — European Commission, Official Journal of the European Union (2023). Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/2379 amending Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 removes stearyl tartrate (E 483) from the list of approved food additives.
